papers.title: Multimodal prehabilitation in colorectal cancer surgery: randomized clinical trial
papers.authors: Bjerregaard F, Pekkari K, Asklid D, Anderin C, Westberg K, Marsk R
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Colorectal cancer (CRC) surgery remains associated with substantial postoperative morbidity despite implementation of enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS). Prehabilitation improves surgical outcomes, but evidence remains inconsistent. This study evaluated whether multidisciplinary prehabilitation reduces postoperative complications and whether treatment effects vary according to baseline physical function.
METHODS: This single-centre randomized clinical trial was conducted at a tertiary referral hospital in Stockholm, Sweden (28 October 2021-23 April 2025). Adults with histologically confirmed CRC scheduled for elective resection were randomized 1 : 1 to multidisciplinary prehabilitation (medication review, nutritional counselling, supervised exercise, and targeted risk optimization) or standard care (ERAS). Analyses followed a modified intention-to-treat (mITT) principle. Prehabilitation was initiated within 3 days of enrolment. The primary outcome of interest was postoperative complications (Clavien-Dindo grade ≥ I). Secondary outcomes included severe complications (Comprehensive Complication Index), reoperations, length of hospital stay (LOS), postoperative weight loss, physical performance and function (6-minute walk test, Timed Up and Go test, and 30-second chair stand test), health-related quality of life (EORTC QLQ-C30), mental health (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale), and correlation with the Disability Rating Index (DRI) score.
RESULTS: Among 328 randomized patients, 242 underwent CRC surgery and were included in the mITT analysis (120 control, 122 intervention). Postoperative complications occurred in 46.2% of patients, with no significant difference between the intervention and control groups (47.5% versus 45.0%, respectively). Severe complications occurred in 19.0% of patients and were numerically less frequent in the intervention group, but the difference was not statistically significant. LOS and reoperation rates were similar. The intervention group had lower postoperative weight loss and modest improvements in physical performance and patient-reported physical function at 30 days. In exploratory analyses, a significant interaction was observed between treatment allocation and baseline DRI score, indicating greater reduction in severe complications among patients with higher levels of preoperative disability (P = 0.011).
CONCLUSIONS: Multidisciplinary prehabilitation did not reduce postoperative complications after CRC surgery. However, exploratory analyses suggest that patients with greater preoperative disability derive greater benefit, supporting targeted prehabilitation strategies in higher-risk populations. Registration number: NCT04909567 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/).

papers.title: Gut microbiota-mediated tryptophan metabolic dysregulation in the comorbidity of inflammatory bowel disease and autism spectrum disorder: mechanisms and research progress
papers.authors: Lu M, Chen Y, Zhou H, Lin Y
papers.abstract: The "microbiota-gut-brain axis" represents a critical link connecting various aspects of intestinal physiology, brain function, and behavioral performance. Among these, tryptophan metabolism abnormalities mediated by gut microbes through the gut-brain axis (GBA) have garnered widespread attention in the study of IBD-ASD comorbidity. This article reviews the current state of research on tryptophan metabolism abnormalities in IBD-ASD comorbidity, with a particular focus on the connection between peripheral and central tryptophan metabolic derangements mediated by gut microbes via the GBA. Furthermore, we summarize and analyze potential therapeutic targets and intervention strategies in this comorbid condition, integrating recent mechanistic studies and clinical evidence to provide a conceptual framework for understanding the potential mechanisms underlying IBD-ASD comorbidity. However, direct evidence from patients with confirmed IBD-ASD comorbidity remains limited at present, and further clinical studies are still needed to test this hypothesis.

papers.title: Clinicopathological, Molecular, and Immune Profiling in Colorectal Cancer: Associations Between KRAS/BRAF Alterations, dMMR/MSI-H Status, and Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Study
papers.authors: Dat N, Minh T, Chu N, Lanh N, Hop H, Cong B
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: To characterize the molecular and immune profiles of resected colorectal cancer (CRC), including KRAS/NRAS/BRAF mutations, deficient mismatch repair/high microsatellite instability (dMMR/MSI-H), and tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) positivity, using routinely available pathological methods, and to identify independent clinicopathological and molecular factors associated with TIL positivity and dMMR/MSI-H status.
METHODS: This retrospective cross-sectional study included 272 patients with primary colorectal adenocarcinoma who underwent surgical resection between 2018 and 2024. KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF mutations were analyzed by real-time polymerase chain reaction. Mismatch repair protein expression was evaluated by immunohistochemistry (IHC), and tumors with loss of at least one mismatch repair protein were classified as dMMR using IHC as a surrogate method for MSI-H status. TIL were assessed on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections.
RESULTS: KRAS mutations were detected in 40.8% of tumors, while BRAF and NRAS mutations were identified in 4.0% and 2.9% of cases, respectively. dMMR/MSI-H was present in 9.6% of tumors. Positive TIL status was observed in 35.3% of cases. Univariable analysis showed that dMMR/MSI-H status and fungating tumor morphology were significantly associated with higher TIL positivity, although these associations became borderline significant after multivariable adjustment. Independent factors associated with dMMR/MSI-H status included younger age (adjusted OR = 0.29, 95% CI: 0.12-0.69), proximal tumor location (adjusted OR = 0.25, 95% CI: 0.10-0.64), and poor tumor differentiation (adjusted OR = 2.80, 95% CI: 1.16-6.76). Subgroup analysis also showed that dMMR-related groups were more likely to have tumors in the proximal colon, poor differentiation, younger age, and higher lymphocytic infiltration.
CONCLUSIONS: Integrated clinicopathological and molecular analysis identified specific CRC features associated with dMMR/MSI-H status, including proximal tumor location, poor differentiation, younger patient age, and a trend toward increased lymphocytic infiltration. Borderline associations were also observed between TIL positivity, fungating tumor morphology, and dMMR/MSI-H phenotypes. These findings support the feasibility of combined molecular and immune evaluation using routinely available pathological methods, particularly in resource-limited settings.

papers.title: Measures of physical fitness and postoperative mortality in patients with colorectal cancer: national cohort study
papers.authors: Rashid A, Blake H, Watton L, Fearnhead N, Han L, van der Meulen J
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Measures of physical fitness are essential for case mix adjustment when comparing surgical outcomes between patient groups, surgical approaches, and healthcare providers. Commonly used measures include clinician-reported American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) grade and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, as well as the Secondary Care Administrative Records Frailty (SCARF) index, derived from routinely collected administrative hospital data. This study compared how these measures of physical fitness, perform for case mix adjustment of postoperative colorectal cancer mortality.
METHODS: All patients diagnosed with colorectal cancer (CRC) between April 2017 and March 2022 in the English and Welsh National Health Service who underwent surgery were included. The primary outcome was 90-day postoperative mortality. Using an established risk-adjustment model, different combinations of ASA grade, performance status, and the SCARF index were added to create eight models for 90-day mortality risk adjustment. Model performance was compared with a full model including all three measures of physical fitness. The basic model included no measures of physical fitness. The scaled Brier score (SBS) measured overall model performance and the C-statistic measured discriminatory ability.
RESULTS: Among 91 957 patients, 90-day mortality was 2.8%. A model including both ASA grade and performance status achieved equivalent performance (SBS 0.092; C-statistic 0.833 (95% confidence interval (c.i.) 0.825 to 0.841)) to the full model (SBS 0.092; C-statistic 0.834 (95% c.i. 0.827 to 0.842)). The basic model with only performance status was slightly inferior (SBS 0.076; C-statistic 0.822 (95% c.i. 0.814 to 0.830)) to the basic model with only ASA grade (SBS 0.084; C-statistic 0.827 (95% c.i. 0.819 to 0.835)).
CONCLUSION: Performance status and ASA grade together accurately adjust for physical fitness when risk adjusting postoperative mortality in patients with CRC. When only one measure is available, performance status or ASA grade alone is suitable to support risk-adjusted hospital benchmarking.

papers.title: Immune remodeling in inflammatory bowel disease-associated colorectal cancer: Mechanisms and immunotherapeutic implications (Review)
papers.authors: Zhang T, Ren Z, Wang L, Man R, Wang L, Wang J
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease‑associated colorectal cancer (IBD‑CRC) arises in the setting of long‑standing chronic intestinal inflammation, in which immune dysregulation cannot be readily attributed to the dominance of a single inhibitory pathway or to global immunosuppression. Persistent inflammatory signaling sustains a state of prolonged immune engagement, yet with constrained effector output, potentially compromising antitumor immune surveillance and limiting the clinical benefit of immunotherapy. The present review synthetises the accumulated knowledge on the long‑term immunological alterations induced by chronic inflammation, including the integration of immune signaling, shifts in activation thresholds, metabolic reprogramming, and functional polarization of immune cells. These changes are discussed in the context of both tumor initiation and tumor maintenance to delineate the immunological evolution of IBD‑CRC. The review further examines the relationship between inflammation‑induced response constraints and the limited efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors, and summarizes the mechanistic barriers to immunotherapy in IBD‑CRC. Collectively, these observations suggest that relieving inhibition through a single target may be insufficient to restore effective antitumor immunity. Finally, the potential value of natural plant‑derived interventions characterized by multi‑component, low‑intensity, and long‑term modulation is discussed, particularly with respect to reducing inflammatory burden and improving immune metabolic states, thereby providing a conceptual basis for the development of combination immunotherapeutic strategies.

papers.title: The molecular pathological basis and potential clinical applications of 'zero-budding' status in stage II colorectal cancer
papers.journal_full: The journal of pathology. Clinical research
papers.authors: Liu Y, Wang B, Xu Q
papers.abstract: In the personalized management of stage II colorectal cancer (CRC), traditional TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) staging has limited ability to accurately stratify the risk of postoperative recurrence. Consequently, oncologists frequently face a major therapeutic dilemma when determining the use of adjuvant chemotherapy in these patients. Although tumor budding (TB) has been incorporated into international clinical guidelines as an independent prognostic marker associated with invasive potential, the conventional International Tumor Budding Consensus Conference classification system is primarily based on routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. Furthermore, this framework classifies tumors with 0-4 buds into a single low-risk category termed Bd1. This classification may obscure important biological differences between tumors with complete absence of cellular dissociation and those already showing early invasive activity. This review proposes separate diagnostic recognition of the 'zero-budding' (Bd0) category. Recent large-scale cohort studies and retrospective analyses support that Bd0 status, particularly when confirmed by pan-cytokeratin immunohistochemistry, is associated with an extremely high negative predictive value for postoperative recurrence. At the subcellular level, the Bd0 category may reflect sustained suppression of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition process. Mechanistically, this relatively non-invasive category may be maintained by preservation of the EBP50 scaffold, which stabilizes the membranous E-cadherin/beta-catenin complex and suppresses nuclear translocation of Wnt/beta-catenin. Bd0 is also strongly associated with the deficient mismatch repair microenvironment, in which high tumor mutational burden may promote enhanced CD8+ T cell-mediated immune surveillance capable of eliminating disseminating tumor cells before morphologic budding becomes detectable. This review summarizes the evolution of TB assessment, reviews the available clinical evidence supporting Bd0, evaluates emerging diagnostic approaches, and discusses the underlying molecular mechanisms.

papers.title: Epidemiological Evidence, Underlying Mechanisms, and Public Health Implications of Ultra-Processed Food Consumption in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: The overall aim of this narrative review is to synthesize epidemiological evidence linking ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption to the onset and progression of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), examine the proposed pathophysiological mechanisms, and evaluate contemporary clinical nutritional strategies. Epidemiological data demonstrates a robust, dose-response association between high UPF intake and an increased risk of incident IBD, predominantly Crohn's disease (CD). Furthermore, in diagnosed patients, UPF consumption correlates with elevated clinical activity, inflammatory relapses, and adverse clinical outcomes. Experimental and observational findings suggest four potential pathways linking UPF-related exposures to altered gut immune homeostasis. First, UPF-rich dietary patterns may be associated with microbiota dysbiosis and reduced short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) availability. Second, experimental studies suggest that selected emulsifiers can alter intestinal mucus organization and epithelial tight-junction integrity. Third, increased intestinal permeability may facilitate exposure to luminal bacterial products and downstream inflammatory signaling through Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) and nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB). Fourth, advanced glycation end products (AGEs) may contribute to intestinal inflammatory signaling and epithelial stress, although their proposed effects on energy sensing and autophagy in IBD require further validation. Current clinical guidance supports healthy dietary patterns with limited UPF intake and individualized nutritional care, while evidence that UPF restriction alone reduces IBD flares remains insufficient. The review concludes that mitigating the clinical burden of IBD requires integrating personalized nutritional interventions managed by specialized dietitians, while highlighting the necessity for further research into specific food additives and precision nutrition strategies.

papers.title: RAS-Pathway Mutation Profiles and Clinical Outcomes Among Patients With Colorectal Cancer
papers.authors: Kazemian E, Liu L, Waissengrin B, Matejcic M, Sobieski D, Tsai Y
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Somatic alterations in the RAS-RAF-MAPK and PI3K pathways are key in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet their distribution, co-occurrence patterns, and clinical significance remain incompletely defined. We characterized RAS/MAPK- and PI3K-pathway alterations in a large cohort and assessed their prognostic implications.
METHODS: We analyzed whole-exome sequencing data from 1243 paired samples from patients with CRC. Somatic variants in KRAS, NRAS, HRAS, BRAF, and PIK3CA were analyzed to quantify frequencies, codon-level distributions, and co-occurrence patterns. Descriptive somatic mutation status and demographic and clinical characteristics were evaluated using chi-square or Fisher exact tests, and associations with overall survival (OS) were evaluated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models.
RESULTS: Any RAS-family mutation was detected in 507 tumors (40.8%); KRAS, NRAS, and HRAS mutations occurred in 35.3%, 5.4%, and 0.6%, respectively. BRAF V600E was detected in 85 tumors (6.8%), PIK3CA in 221 (17.8%), and KRAS G12C in 38 (3.1%). KRAS codon 12 was the dominant RAS hotspot. KRAS-PIK3CA co-mutations occurred in 126 tumors (10.1% overall; 28.7% of KRAS-mutant tumors), whereas KRAS-BRAF and KRAS-NRAS co-mutations were uncommon, consistent with MAPK pathway mutual exclusivity. RAS-mutant tumors were enriched in right-sided and microsatellite-stable disease (p < 0.001 for both). KRAS, BRAF V600E, and PIK3CA mutation frequencies were higher in right-sided than left-sided tumors. In unadjusted analyses, Hispanic patients had lower KRAS, BRAF V600E, and PIK3CA mutation frequencies than non-Hispanic patients. After adjustment for age, sex, tumor location, and MSI status, the associations with KRAS and PIK3CA were attenuated, whereas the lower frequency of BRAF V600E among Hispanic patients persisted (p < 0.01). Mutation status was not significantly associated with 5-year overall survival.
CONCLUSIONS: RAS/MAPK and PI3K pathway alterations in CRC varied primarily by tumor subtype and molecular context, with clinically relevant co-mutation patterns and a targetable KRAS G12C subset. These findings may support future clinical trials targeting the BRAF-RAS axis.
